connector: The soldiers are gone, but nobody believes they are finished. Before the sun is fully up, the family has a plan, and Papa makes a phone call that sounds perfectly ordinary. As you read, ask what Papa’s words might really mean, and why a family would need to talk in a kind of code.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Grete. After the soldiers leave, nobody in the Johansen family sleeps. By the end of this chapter, they’re on a train going north, and Papa has made a very strange phone call. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 6, and study one sentence the way a writer would. Today’s question: why do people speak carefully when danger is near?
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move is about choosing small. When you prove a point, you don’t need the whole scene. You need the few exact words that do the job. As you read, listen for a short phrase a grown-up says, one you could copy word for word to show courage.
transcripts.dol: The model is about a trip. The sentence to fix is really two sentences run together. Find where one complete thought ends and the next one begins. Then check the name at the very start, because names always stand up tall.
transcripts.guide1: Today the word work asks you to hunt for two things at once. In grammar, you’ll find both the person-word and the action that goes with it. In spelling, you’ll catch pieces added at the front and pieces added at the end. Keep both in your head as you go.
transcripts.morphology: Two more reaches of light across the water. The roots are the same, believing and stretching, but the words are new. One of them is about papers that prove who you are. That mattered a great deal in 1943. Read each meaning carefully before you choose.
transcripts.vocabulary: In the last lesson you met these four words with a sentence and a flip card. Now see if they stuck. Match each word to its meaning. If you miss one, don’t worry. Read the meaning again, and say it to yourself in your own words.
transcripts.grammar: Some of these sentences have a name doing the action, and some have a pronoun. Only the pronouns and their verbs count today. That’s the tricky part. Before you tap, ask yourself: is this a little stand-in word, or is it a person’s name?
transcripts.spelling: This sentence is a short trip on the train. Hunt for words with an extra piece on the front, and words with an extra piece on the end. One word even has two pieces on the end. Careful: a word that only looks built doesn’t count.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about the grown-ups. Mama doesn’t make a speech. She just packs, smiles, and gets three girls on a train. My own mother was like that. When she was most worried, she talked about the weather and buttered our bread. It took me years to understand that her calm was her courage.
transcripts.read: Listen closely to Papa on the telephone. Every word he says sounds ordinary. Ask what it might really mean, and notice how Annemarie starts to wonder too. Then you’ll ride the train north along the sea. Keep an eye on the door at the end of the train car.
transcripts.rwm: Read this sentence again, slowly. The writer doesn’t stop to print the whole phone call. She keeps her own sentence moving and tucks Papa’s words inside it. That’s a trick you can borrow for your essay, when you want to share what someone said without dropping in a big, clunky quote.
transcripts.guide3: Now it’s your turn to write. The questions ask about the family’s plan, why Papa talks the way he does, and what Ellen has to leave behind. Then you’ll write the opening of your essay: a hook that drops the reader into a moment, and your claim.
transcripts.chapter: The middle question asks why Papa speaks almost in code. To answer it, think about who else might hear a telephone call in 1943. Then think about Ellen. What does it cost a ten-year-old to say goodbye without knowing when she’ll see her parents again?
transcripts.workshop: An introduction does two jobs. First it pulls the reader in with a real moment from the book. Then it says plainly what you believe. Keep it short. A confident first paragraph of three sentences beats a long one that wanders.

a.raw: papa speaks in code on the phone the soldiers may be listening to him
a.fixed: Papa speaks in code on the phone. The soldiers may be listening to him.
a.why: A capital P on Papa, a period after phone, a capital T to start the second sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: mama takes the girls on the train they are going to gilleleje
b.fixed: Mama takes the girls on the train. They are going to Gilleleje.
b.why: A capital M on Mama, a period after train, a capital T to start the second sentence, a capital G on Gilleleje, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why the plan has to happen so quickly.
scholar.journal-q2: … and give one example of an ordinary word that might secretly mean something else.
scholar.journal-q3: … and compare what Ellen gives up with what the Johansens risk.

match.intend: Intend has the root that means stretch. Look for the meaning about planning to do something on purpose.
match.credible: Credible has the root that means believe. Look for the meaning about being easy to believe.
match.discreet: Discreet is about being careful and quiet. Look for the meaning about not drawing attention.
match.tense: Tense is a feeling in your body. Look for the meaning about being tight with worry.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Each stretching word reaches the light across the water; each believing word lights a window on the far shore.

why.t: In Chapter 7, Annemarie stands on the shore at Gilleleje and points across the sea to Sweden. tend means to stretch, so each right tend word stretches the lighthouse beam a little farther across the water. cred means to believe, so each right cred word lights a window on the far shore. One stretch of water each lesson, until the light reaches Sweden.

miss.fill1: Not quite. tend means stretch. Is credentials about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill2: Not quite. tend means stretch. Is discredit about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill3: Not quite. cred means believe. Is contend about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill4: Not quite. cred means believe. Is tendon about believing, or about stretching?

wordgame.winDay: Halfway across. Four windows glow on the far shore now. The next lesson’s words stretch the beam farther still.
wordgame.win: The light reaches all the way across the water, and on the far shore, Kullen’s lighthouse answers. cred = believe, tend = stretch.

notes.wgrd: Good evidence is short and exact. Choose only the few words that prove your point, copy them letter for letter inside quotation marks, and wrap them in your own sentence.
vocab: To plan to do something on purpose.
notes.wordParts: cred means “to believe” (credible, incredible). tend means “to stretch” or “to reach” (extend, pretend, attend).
notes.grammar: A pronoun and its verb must agree. With he, she or it, the verb takes an s: she watches, he listens. With I, you, we or they, it doesn’t: they wait.
notes.spelling: Many long words are built from parts: a prefix in front (un-, re-, dis-), a base word, and a suffix at the end (-ful, -ly, -ness, -ance). Find the base underneath and keep its spelling: hope + ful + ly = hopefully.

case.title: A Telephone in Code
case.alt: A heavy black telephone with a round number dial and a handset resting on top, on a wooden table.
label: This black telephone is made of bakelite, an early kind of hard plastic. Phones like it were first made in 1931 by the Swedish company Ericsson, and they sat in homes all over Scandinavia.

During the occupation, people knew someone might be listening to a phone call. So they spoke in ordinary words that meant something else. In Chapter 6, Papa asks Uncle Henrik about the weather for fishing, and Annemarie can tell he is speaking almost in code.

look.q: How do you think you made a call on a phone like this?
look.a: You put a finger in a hole on the round dial and turned it, once for every number. Then you held the heavy handset to your ear.

look.q: Why would a family be careful about what they said on the phone?
look.a: The Germans could listen in. One careless word could put a whole family, and their friends, in danger.

case.credit: Ericsson bakelite telephone, 1931 design. Photo: Holger Ellgaard, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
case.sub: A real object from the war years.
